title: Europe Wants Digital Sovereignty. It Needs the Talent to Build It.
summary: As Europe accelerates investment in digital sovereignty and sovereign cloud infrastructure, organizations need more than technology to maintain control.
body_markdown:
Across Europe, digital sovereignty has moved from an abstract national policy debate to a boardroom priority. In fact, in our recent


[Experis 2026 CIO Outlook](https://www.experis.com/en/cio-outlook) , most CIOs (69%) told us digital sovereignty was their second highest priority for 2026 IT budget increases.


In my conversations with clients across financial services, energy, manufacturing and the public sector, I hear the same questions repeatedly:


-


Where is our data stored?


-


Who controls it?


-


How resilient is our infrastructure?


-


And do we have the skills to operate it securely and at scale?


These are no longer theoretical questions. They are influencing cloud investment, vendor strategies and operating models. And behind these questions lies a broader challenge for business leaders:


## **D oes owning or procuring infrastructure give an organization the capability to control it?**


Investment is an essential starting point, but meaningful control depends on people. Organizations need the skills and knowledge to operate their infrastructure, understand its dependencies and make informed decisions about its future. This is particularly important as 75% of information technology employers around the world tell us they are


[struggling to find the skilled talent they need](https://www.manpowergroup.com/en/insights/2026-global-talent-shortage) .


## **Greater control still requires global capability**


Europe's digital ambitions are bringing this challenge into sharper focus. Businesses are being asked to accelerate technology adoption while strengthening control over the infrastructure that enables it.


The


[European Commission's 2030 Digital Decade objectives](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cloud-computing) include having 75% of European enterprises use cloud-edge technologies and deploying 10,000 climate-neutral and highly secure edge nodes across Europe.


Achieving those ambitions will require more than infrastructure. It will also depend on how effectively organizations access and develop specialist expertise.


CIOs prioritize digital sovereignty:


[Experis research](https://www.experis.com/en/cio-outlook) found most CIOs (81%) identified digital sovereignty as a high priority, while 67% expect to increase offshore or nearshore delivery.


These findings may appear contradictory: leaders want greater sovereignty while expanding their use of cross-border delivery. In practice, they reflect the balance organizations are trying to achieve.


Greater control over technology does not remove the need for global talent. European organizations still need access to specialized capabilities wherever they are available. The goal is therefore not to eliminate every external dependency, bring every specialist in-house or step away from global technology ecosystems.


Instead, leaders need to build controlled interdependence. That means benefiting from global technology and expertise while retaining the knowledge, capability and decision-making authority to remain in control.


## **Investment momentum raises the stakes**


The investment outlook underscores the scale of this opportunity—and the importance of getting the workforce strategy right.


[Gartner forecasts](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-02-09-gartner-says-worldwide-sovereign-cloud-iaas-spending-will-total-us-dollars-80-billion-in-2026) that European spending on sovereign cloud infrastructure will rise from $6.9 billion in 2025 to $12.6 billion in 2026 and $23.1 billion in 2027.


These figures are projections, not realized spending. But even with that distinction, the forecast signals the scale of infrastructure investment anticipated across Europe. The next challenge is turning that investment into resilience and operational control. This is where technology strategy and workforce


strategy


need to come together.


## **The sovereignty gap is also a skills gap**


For organizations in regulated industries, the gap between ambition and execution becomes clear as implementation begins. Choosing a cloud environment, setting data-residency requirements and putting contractual and regulatory safeguards in place establish the foundations. People turn those foundations into a working capability.


-


Who will design the architecture?


-


Who will keep the environment secure?


-


Who will integrate it with existing systems?


-


Who will understand its dependencies well enough to assess and challenge provider recommendations?


-


And how will critical knowledge be retained when external specialists or project teams move on?


Together, these questions reveal whether an organization simply owns infrastructure or has the capability to control it. Our


[Experis research](https://www.experis.com/en/cio-outlook) highlights the skills at the center of that challenge. CIOs across Europe and North America told us Cybersecurity (46%), AI & machine learning (37%), and Cloud computing were the most in-demand tech skills their teams need.


**CIOs share top 3 tech skills gaps**

computing (

Yet demand for these capabilities is competing with persistent talent shortages. These are global findings, not Europe-specific measures, but they provide important context for the competition for technology skills.


Skills are not the only constraint. Infrastructure, capital, security and regulation also shape what organizations can achieve. But the workforce implication is clear. Investment in infrastructure must go hand in hand with investment in people and capability.


Without the expertise to operate, secure, understand and evolve a sovereign cloud environment, organizations risk falling short of the autonomy they set out to achieve.


## **E xternal expertise should build lasting capability**


This creates an important opportunity for technology partners and workforce specialists to help organizations meet today's needs while building the capability they will need tomorrow. External expertise should strengthen autonomy, rather than create a new dependency.


Success should be measured not only by what an engagement delivers, but by the capability it leaves behind. For workforce planning, that means looking beyond the immediate question of what skills to bring in and giving equal attention to capabilities they will need over time.


## **F our CIO priorities to shift the focus to long-term growth**


-


Build knowledge transfer into delivery:


Critical technical and operational knowledge must become part of the organization, not remain solely with the external project team. Making knowledge transfer a priority from the outset helps turn it into an ongoing part of delivery, rather than an activity left to the final handover.


-


Make documentation usable:


Documentation has value when it enables people to act. Internal teams need clear, practical resources they can use to understand, operate and evolve the


environment—


not simply a record that the project is complete.


-


Establish clear accountability:


Internal teams, technology vendors and specialist partners need a shared understanding of who is accountable for architecture, security, operational decisions and outcomes. As delivery ecosystems become more complex, that clarity becomes more important.


-


Measure outcomes that demonstrate capability:


Deploying specialists and reaching technical go-live are important milestones. They do not, on their own, demonstrate that an organization has built lasting capability.


These four priorities are meant to be leveraged as a practical framework, rather than measures drawn from the cited research. But the key takeaway is to find partners that simultaneously increase your organization’s digital autonomy.


## **The CIO's new role: orchestrating sovereignty and capability**


For CIOs, this brings the connection between technology leadership and workforce leadership into sharper focus. The strategic task is to align technology choices with the people and capabilities needed to turn them into business outcomes.


That requires deliberate decisions about where capability should reside:


-


What does the organization need to own?


-


What must it understand to retain control?


-


Which skills should be developed internally?


-


Where can specialist partners accelerate delivery?


-


Where can cross-border delivery provide expertise that is difficult to access locally?


-


And what knowledge must be transferred back before an external engagement is complete?


Answering these questions takes a blend of hiring, internal development and specialist support.


External candidates remain the leading source of experienced technology talent, while internal promotion and outsourced IT services have gained popularity since 2025.


For Europe's technology leaders, infrastructure investment must go hand in hand with investment in people. Alongside data location, security, regulation and vendor choice, autonomy requires the expertise to operate, secure and evolve technology and guide its future.


Partners such as Experis can help turn immediate delivery into lasting capability through knowledge transfer, practical documentation and clear


accountability—


leaving internal teams stronger and more autonomous.


Ultimately, digital sovereignty means managing dependencies, not eliminating them. Investing in people and skills enables organizations to draw on global expertise while retaining


control—


turning technology ownership into meaningful autonomy.
